SLIDES:

a little + uncountable = a small amount, and that is fine.

She has a few dinners with friends a year.

much + uncountable, mostly in negatives and questions.

How many decisions do you make without noticing?

many + countable plural, mostly in negatives and questions.

too much = more than is good. not enough = less than you need.

Stage 3 · Grammar

How much, how many, and how to say “too”

Every choice here starts with one question: can you count the noun?

Read these four sentences from the text in stage 5.
  • She puts a little money aside every month.
  • She has a few dinners with friends a year.
  • There isn’t much left at the end of the month.
  • He wastes a lot of money on things he forgets.
Why is it a little money but a few dinners?
Countable, uncountable, and the words that go with each
Countable — coins, bills, dinnersUncountable — money, time, advice
A small amounta few coinsa little money
A large amounta lot of / lots of coinsa lot of / lots of money
Negative & questionnot many coins · How many coins?not much money · How much money?
More than is goodtoo many billstoo much money
The right amountenough — works with both: enough coins, enough money. Less than you need → not enough.
some / anysome in positives and offers; any in negatives and most questions: I have some money · I don’t have any money · Would you like some tea?
Articles recycleda credit card · the bill you told me about · made of — plastic
The rules that matter
  • First ask: can I put a number in front of the noun? three coins yes, three moneys no. That single question decides much/many, a little/a few and too much/too many.
  • money, time, information, advice, news, work are uncountable in English even though your language may count them.
  • In a positive sentence prefer a lot of: say I have a lot of work, not I have much work. much and many live mostly in negatives and questions.
  • too much / too many means it is a problem. not enough means there is less than you need. They are opposites.
  • You met articles in Lesson 13. They come back in task 5 of the next stage.
Full grammar reference — Quantifiers

Form

Countablea few · many · not many · too many · a lot of · some / any
Uncountablea little · much · not much · too much · a lot of · some / any
QuestionsHow many coins? · How much money?
Positive / negativesome in positive sentences; any in negatives and most questions
Enoughenough money · not enough time · the word goes before the noun

When and why we use it

  • Countable nouns can be counted one by one (coins, bills, notes); uncountable nouns cannot (money, time, work, advice).
  • A few and a little mean ‘a small amount, but some’. Without a, the meaning becomes negative: few friends = almost none.
  • Too much / too many = more than is good. Not enough = less than is needed.
  • Some also appears in questions when you offer or request: Would you like some tea?

Signal words

How much…? · How many…? · far too much · not nearly enough

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • How much coins have you got? → How many coins…?Coins can be counted.
  • I have too much friends. → I have too many friends.Countable.
  • There isn’t some milk. → There isn’t any milk.Any in negatives.
  • I don’t have enough of money. → I don’t have enough money.No of before the noun.

Don’t confuse it with

a few (some, and that is fine) against few (almost none, and that is a problem). The same for a little and little.

Stage 5 · Main input

Three ways to be wrong about money

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read. Three people are described. What do you think they have in common?

Three ways to be wrong about money

Ask three people how they manage their money and you will get three different answers — and all three will tell you they are doing it right.

Aizhan is a saver. She transfers a little money into a savings account every month, she never has any debt, and she checks her balance almost every day. She has enough for an emergency. But she also says no to almost everything: a few dinners with friends a year, no holidays, no small treats. Her sister says she saves too much and lives too little.

Timur is the opposite. He earns a good salary, but there isn’t much left at the end of the month. He can’t tell you where it goes — a coffee here, a taxi there. He has a credit card, and now he owes the bank a lot of money. Every year he promises to pay it back. Every year he doesn’t.

Then there is Marat, who is careful with big things and careless with small ones. He spent months choosing a cheap flat, and he pays a low rent. But he wastes money on things he forgets: three streaming services he never watches, a gym with a monthly fee he has used twice, a jacket he never sent back for a refund.

You can measure a salary. You cannot easily measure the money that leaves quietly, in small amounts, without a decision — and no statistic on Timur’s bank app will tell him where it went.

Most of us are one of these three. The interesting question is not how much you earn. It is how many decisions you make without noticing — and whether there is enough left when you finally do.

Note. Written for this course as a reading text. Aizhan, Timur and Marat are invented, and no words are attributed to a real person. The text makes no statistical claim and quotes no survey.
